content: 1. It is essential to contribute to the completeness of National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) data while ensuring the protection of individuals and maintaining the confidentiality of their data. 2. Supervisory visits to all tuberculosis (TB) service centers should be conducted regularly. The frequency of these visits should be determined by the emergency setting, available resources, and the schedule established by the coordination structure. 3. Community leaders should be included in the supervision team to ensure community acceptance of the TB program. 4. A sample checklist, such as the one provided in Annex 4, can assist less experienced staff in conducting TB supervision visits, either independently or in collaboration with other programs. 5. TB should be included as part of the essential services reviewed during evaluations of humanitarian settings. These evaluations should adhere to United Nations standards and guidelines, aiming for an impartial analysis of both expected and unexpected outcomes, as well as the relevance, context, and impact of emergency operations. 6. The primary agency responsible for emergency operations should determine the timing of evaluations based on the level of the emergency. These evaluations should involve all key stakeholders, apply specific terms of reference, analyze both primary and secondary data, and include public reporting. 7. Time and resource constraints often limit evaluations to essential operations and services, including TB services, which should be assessed as part of the overall quality of healthcare provided at all levels, taking into account the social determinants of the affected population. 8. Periodic external reviews of TB services in emergency settings are critical. These reviews may be part of comprehensive NTP reviews or conducted ad hoc due to changes in humanitarian operations, the need for additional resources, or requests from the emergency coordination structure. 9. All relevant stakeholders should participate in evaluating TB interventions in relation to overall emergency operations and the need for long-term sustainable solutions. 10. Engaging communities, civil society organizations, and community health providers is a crucial first step in addressing barriers to TB service delivery. This includes analyzing the situation to identify barriers, assessing the feasibility of community-based TB activities, and determining the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of such interventions. 11. Based on the analysis, specific community-based activities can be assigned, such as referring individuals diagnosed with TB for continued treatment, supporting treatment adherence through peer support and education, providing home-based care, assisting with infection control measures, and raising awareness to reduce stigma and discrimination. 12. Community health workers and volunteers play a vital role in TB prevention, treatment, and care at the community level. Their capacity should be enhanced through formal or informal education, training, and mentoring, with clear job descriptions provided. 13. Populations affected by emergencies may include individuals with medical education who can be employed to support TB interventions. Community-based TB activities should be monitored using specific indicators to assess inputs, processes, outputs, outcomes, and impacts, with results reported back to the community, donors, and other stakeholders. 14. Two essential indicators for monitoring community-based TB interventions are: (i) the percentage of TB cases diagnosed after referral by community health workers or volunteers, and (ii) the percentage of TB cases successfully treated with the support of community health workers or volunteers. 15. Effective TB risk communication should be coordinated by the central emergency coordination structure, tailored to updated needs, and aligned with professionalism and evidence-based practices. Communication strategies should adapt to different phases of the emergency and target audiences, with activities and tools developed and implemented accordingly. 16. Research during the acute phase of an emergency may focus on documenting the experiences of those affected by TB, identifying good practices, and designing comprehensive care and communication strategies. 17. In humanitarian settings, operational research on strategies, interventions, tools, or knowledge to improve program performance and healthcare delivery is often the most appropriate. Research activities should be agreed upon by all stakeholders, including affected communities, and conducted under the supervision of national or international ethical committees. 18. Preliminary research results should be shared with stakeholders before publication to improve services for affected populations and their host communities. Success in research requires clear questions and plans, dedicated staff and resources, well-maintained databases, and translation of findings into policy and practice. 19. Durable solutions for refugees and displaced persons with TB, such as voluntary repatriation, local integration, or resettlement, should prioritize their medical needs. Access to effective health services during transit and upon arrival at the destination must be ensured. 20. Individuals undergoing TB treatment should receive special attention, with decisions made in accordance with ethical principles of autonomy. Preparations for repatriation, resettlement, or relocation should include appraising the health system of the destination country, informing the individual about available TB services, and ensuring the continuity of treatment. 21. Drug-resistant TB cases require additional considerations, such as ensuring the availability of appropriate drugs, laboratory monitoring, and patient support. Transfer processes should be short, under medical supervision, and include formal agreements with the receiving country or service. 22. The phasing out or handover of emergency TB operations should be planned carefully to ensure a smooth transition. This includes clarifying how individuals already on treatment will complete it and determining when and how to discontinue diagnostic and treatment services. 23. Sharing patient data between countries should respect national policies and data protection principles. Informed consent from individuals is essential, and data should be collected for specific, legitimate purposes, ensuring accuracy, confidentiality, and limited storage duration. 24. Mechanisms for data sharing may include direct communication between NTP managers, mediation by organizations such as WHO or UNHCR, or regional systems. These mechanisms should ensure data protection while facilitating the continuation of treatment and care for individuals with TB.
